questions.q: Which feature most reliably distinguishes COPD from asthma?
ch: Airflow limitation that is not fully reversible
questions.exp: COPD is defined by persistent airflow limitation that is not fully reversible; asthma's obstruction is reversible. This is the central contrast between the two.
why: Smoking is the dominant cause of COPD but many smokers never develop it and some COPD patients never smoked.
Nocturnal worsening is more characteristic of asthma.
Inhaled corticosteroids help selected COPD patients, so a response does not exclude COPD.
Wheeze occurs in both and does not separate them.

questions.q: Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically as a productive cough for:
ch: Any duration if sputum is purulent
At least 2 weeks in a single year
At least 1 month in a single year
At least 3 months per year for 2 consecutive years
At least 6 months in a single year
questions.exp: Chronic bronchitis is a clinical definition: a productive cough for at least 3 months per year over 2 consecutive years.
why: Purulence indicates infection or exacerbation, not the chronic bronchitis definition.
Two weeks describes an acute bronchitis, not the chronic phenotype.
One month is far short of the definition.
Six months in one year still does not meet the two-consecutive-year requirement.

questions.q: Which test is required to establish a diagnosis of COPD?
ch: Arterial blood gas showing CO2 retention
Spirometry with a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70
questions.exp: Spirometry is required. A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 confirms persistent airflow limitation; COPD should not be diagnosed on clinical grounds alone.
why: Chronic respiratory acidosis reflects severity, not diagnosis.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin is checked selectively in young or non-smoking patients, not to diagnose COPD.
Oximetry measures oxygenation and says nothing about airflow limitation.
Hyperinflation and flattened diaphragms support the diagnosis but do not establish it.

questions.q: What is the appropriate oxygen saturation target in a patient with COPD?
ch: Whatever is needed to abolish all dyspnea
questions.exp: Target SpO2 88-92%. Over-oxygenation risks worsening hypercapnia; oxygen should never be withheld from a hypoxic patient, but it must be titrated.
why: Driving saturation above 98% risks CO2 retention.
94-98% is the general adult target, not the COPD target.
80-85% leaves the patient dangerously hypoxemic.
Dyspnea is not the titration endpoint; oxygen is titrated to a saturation range.

questions.q: A patient presents with an acute COPD exacerbation and increased sputum purulence and volume. Which combination is most appropriate?
ch: Short-acting bronchodilators, systemic steroids, and antibiotics
questions.exp: Exacerbations are treated with short-acting bronchodilators, a short course of systemic steroids, and antibiotics when sputum purulence and volume increase, alongside controlled oxygen.
why: Long-acting bronchodilators are maintenance therapy, not rescue.
Targeting 100% saturation risks worsening hypercapnia.
Inhaled corticosteroids are not monotherapy in COPD and do not treat an acute exacerbation.
Antibiotics address the infective trigger but leave the bronchospasm and inflammation untreated.

questions.q: What is the role of non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) in an acute hypercapnic COPD exacerbation?
ch: It reduces the need for intubation and reduces mortality
It is used only after intubation has failed
It is reserved for patients who are already comatose
It has no proven benefit over oxygen alone
It is contraindicated because it worsens air trapping
questions.exp: NIV is the workhorse of acute hypercapnic COPD exacerbations: it reduces intubation rates and mortality, and should be reached for early.
why: NIV is used to prevent intubation, not as a post-failure measure.
A comatose patient generally cannot protect the airway and needs intubation; NIV is used earlier.
The mortality and intubation benefit is well established.
NIV is beneficial, not contraindicated, in hypercapnic exacerbation.

questions.q: Which two interventions have been shown to prolong survival in COPD?
ch: Smoking cessation and long-term oxygen therapy in chronically hypoxemic patients
questions.exp: Only smoking cessation and long-term oxygen therapy in chronically hypoxemic patients clearly prolong survival. Everything else is symptom control.
why: These are adjuncts with no established mortality benefit.
These treat exacerbations; they do not modify long-term survival.
Both improve symptoms and exacerbation frequency but are not the survival-modifying pair.
Bronchodilators and vaccines reduce symptoms and exacerbations without a clear survival benefit.

questions.q: A 38-year-old who has never smoked is diagnosed with emphysema. Which investigation is most important?
questions.exp: Emphysema in a young or non-smoking patient should prompt measurement of alpha-1 antitrypsin, an inherited cause of early emphysema.
why: Sweat chloride tests for cystic fibrosis, which presents differently and far earlier.
Sinus imaging does not explain emphysema.
IgE and eosinophils point toward allergic asthma rather than emphysema.
Methacholine challenge tests for airway hyperresponsiveness in suspected asthma.

questions.q: How is the blood eosinophil count used in modern COPD management?
ch: To confirm the diagnosis of COPD without spirometry
To decide whether a patient is likely to benefit from an inhaled corticosteroid
To determine the target oxygen saturation range
To grade disease severity in place of spirometry
To decide the duration of antibiotic therapy
questions.exp: Eosinophil count now helps identify which patients benefit from inhaled corticosteroids, letting you justify or withhold them on a guideline basis.
why: Diagnosis requires spirometry, not a blood count.
The oxygen target is 88-92% regardless of eosinophils.
Severity is graded by FEV1 percent predicted and GOLD groups.
Antibiotic duration is guided by clinical response, not eosinophils.

questions.q: A COPD patient on oxygen becomes progressively drowsy. What is the most appropriate next step?
ch: Obtain an urgent CT of the head
questions.exp: Increasing drowsiness on oxygen suggests CO2 retention. Check an arterial blood gas rather than simply increasing oxygen; rising CO2 with declining consciousness signals impending respiratory failure.
why: Increasing oxygen may worsen the hypercapnia that is causing the drowsiness.
Sedation would further depress ventilation in a patient already retaining CO2.
Oxygen should be titrated, never abruptly withdrawn from a hypoxic patient.
Imaging delays recognition of a metabolic cause that a blood gas identifies immediately.

questions.q: Which feature defines asthma and separates it from COPD?
questions.exp: Reversibility is the defining feature of asthma: bronchoconstriction, mucosal edema and mucus plugging that improve with bronchodilator.
why: A productive cough is more characteristic of chronic bronchitis.
Chronic CO2 retention is a COPD feature, not a defining asthma feature.
Barrel chest reflects the air trapping of emphysema.
Alveolar destruction describes emphysema and is irreversible.

questions.q: Which spirometric result demonstrates reversibility and supports a diagnosis of asthma?
ch: A total lung capacity above predicted
A normal spirometry result on a single occasion
A fall in FEV1 of 12% after bronchodilator
An FEV1 improvement of at least 12% and 200 mL after bronchodilator
An FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70 that does not change
questions.exp: Reversibility is demonstrated when FEV1 improves by at least 12% and 200 mL after a bronchodilator. Prove the diagnosis with these numbers rather than describing wheeze.
why: Increased total lung capacity reflects hyperinflation, not reversibility.
Normal spirometry does not exclude asthma; consider bronchoprovocation testing.
A fall in FEV1 after bronchodilator is not reversibility.
A fixed ratio that does not change describes irreversible obstruction, favouring COPD.

questions.q: Which medication is the cornerstone controller therapy for persistent asthma?
ch: Leukotriene receptor antagonist as sole therapy
questions.exp: The inhaled corticosteroid is the cornerstone of controller therapy in persistent asthma, taken daily even when the patient feels well.
why: A long-acting beta-agonist must never be used alone in asthma.
Theophylline is an older adjunct with a narrow therapeutic window.
A leukotriene antagonist is an add-on or alternative, not the cornerstone.
A short-acting beta-agonist is a reliever; frequent use signals poor control rather than providing it.

questions.q: During an acute asthma attack the wheeze diminishes markedly while the patient's distress worsens. What does this indicate?
ch: The patient has developed a pneumothorax
Air movement has become dangerously reduced
questions.exp: A silent chest is an emergency: it means almost no air is moving, not that the patient is improving. Prepare for escalation and possible intubation.
why: Pneumothorax is possible but the classic meaning of a quiet chest with rising distress is critically reduced airflow.
Effective treatment relieves distress; here distress is worsening.
Hyperventilation would increase, not reduce, audible air movement.
Diminishing wheeze with worsening distress is deterioration, not resolution.

questions.q: An arterial blood gas during a severe asthma attack shows a PaCO2 that has risen from low to normal. How should this be interpreted?
ch: Reassuring, as the gas is now normal
A sign the patient is tiring toward respiratory failure
An expected effect of supplemental oxygen
A laboratory error requiring a repeat sample
questions.exp: A normalizing or rising PaCO2 in an acute attack is ominous. The patient who was hyperventilating is now fatiguing, and this warrants ICU-level care.
why: A 'normal' CO2 in a patient who should be blowing it off is a red flag, not reassurance.
Bronchodilators do not cause CO2 to rise in this pattern.
Supplemental oxygen does not explain fatigue-driven CO2 retention in asthma.
The finding fits the clinical picture and should be acted on, not dismissed.

questions.q: Why must a long-acting beta-agonist never be prescribed as monotherapy in asthma?
ch: It increases the risk of death in asthma
It is less effective than a short-acting agent
It is only licensed for use in COPD
questions.exp: LABA monotherapy increases mortality in asthma. A long-acting beta-agonist must always be paired with an inhaled corticosteroid.
why: Effectiveness is not the issue; the safety signal is.
Thrush is an inhaled corticosteroid effect, prevented by rinsing the mouth.
LABAs are used in asthma, but only in combination with an inhaled corticosteroid.
Tremor is a nuisance effect of beta-agonists generally and is not the reason for the restriction.

questions.q: A patient reports using their rescue inhaler every day. What does this most likely represent?
ch: Tolerance to beta-agonists requiring a higher dose
A need to stop the inhaled corticosteroid
questions.exp: Daily rescue inhaler use, or more than two canisters a year, predicts exacerbations and should be treated as under-controlled inflammation rather than a dosing problem.
why: Frequent reliever use is a marker of failed control, not success.
A reliever is for occasional symptoms; daily need signals poor control.
The answer is not to increase the beta-agonist but to address the underlying inflammation.
Stopping the controller would worsen control.

questions.q: A patient's asthma remains uncontrolled despite an appropriate inhaled corticosteroid prescription. What should be checked before escalating drug therapy?
questions.exp: Poor inhaler technique and non-adherence are leading causes of apparently uncontrolled asthma. Check these systematically before adding drugs.
why: Imaging is reasonable later, but technique and adherence come first.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema, not refractory asthma.
A blood gas assesses an acute attack, not chronic control.
Theophylline levels are only relevant if the patient is taking it.

questions.q: Which modern approach does GINA favour over short-acting beta-agonist-only treatment?
ch: Leukotriene antagonist monotherapy for all patients
Inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol as combined controller and reliever
questions.exp: GINA has shifted away from SABA-only treatment toward inhaled corticosteroid-containing therapy, including ICS-formoterol used as both maintenance and reliever in a single inhaler.
why: Leukotriene antagonists are an option for some patients but not a universal replacement.
Intermittent oral steroids carry cumulative toxicity and are not a control strategy.
LABA monotherapy is precisely what the safety rationale forbids.
Theophylline is not first-line in modern guidance.

questions.q: A patient in an acute attack has a peak expiratory flow below 50% of personal best that is not responding to treatment, with exhaustion and altered mentation. What does this represent?
ch: An expected response to nebulized therapy
A moderate exacerbation suitable for discharge with oral steroids
Life-threatening asthma requiring preparation for intubation
Vocal cord dysfunction rather than asthma
questions.exp: Exhaustion, cyanosis or altered mentation with a peak flow below 50% of personal best that is not responding defines life-threatening asthma; prepare for intubation.
why: Failure to respond is the concerning feature.
Altered mentation in this setting reflects respiratory failure, not anxiety.
This combination is far beyond a moderate exacerbation and is not safe for discharge.
Vocal cord dysfunction can mimic asthma but does not explain this degree of objective airflow limitation with exhaustion.
